# Marcus "Moose" Okoro

**Background & Personality:**
Moose is sixteen, lives with both parents and his younger sister Tia (fourteen, insufferable, currently in a phase where she refers to everything as "iconic" or "a red flag") in a slightly nicer semi-detached two streets over from Leo's. His mum is a district nurse; his dad works at the Jaguar Land Rover plant in Solihull and comes home smelling of machine oil and quiet exhaustion. The Okoro household is warm, busy, and organized in a way that Leo's isn't—there's a chore rota on the fridge, family dinners on Sundays, and his dad makes jollof rice on Saturdays that fills the whole house with the smell of tomato and scotch bonnet.

Moose earned his nickname in Year 7 when he got stuck in a doorframe during a fire drill—not because he was large, but because he panicked and tried to go through sideways. The name stuck because it was funny, and Moose accepted it with the pragmatism that defines him. His real name is Marcus, and only his mum and his form tutor use it.

He is anxious. This is not a cute, quirky anxiety—it's a real, physiological thing that manifests as a tightness in his chest before social situations, a tendency to catastrophize, and a near-compulsive need to plan for worst-case scenarios. He manages it. He breathes. He makes lists. He has a CBT worksheet on his phone that he's supposed to fill in daily and mostly doesn't. But it's there, and it shapes everything—his caution, his need for control, his occasional rigidity.

But here's the thing about Moose that Leo doesn't always see: he's also quietly fierce. He has opinions and he holds them. He once argued with a supply teacher for twenty minutes about the accuracy of a historical timeline, calmly and with evidence, until the teacher gave up. He doesn't back down when he thinks he's right, which makes him both admirable and occasionally infuriating. He is the moral compass of the pair, and like all moral compasses, he's not always pointing where you want him to.

**Core Details:**
- Keeps a suspect list in his phone's notes app with colour-coded confidence ratings (red = high, amber = medium, green = "probably not but can't rule out"). The system is meticulous and slightly unhinged.
- Brilliant at maths. Not in a prodigy way, but in a "gets A* and makes it look effortless" way. He doesn't flaunt it, but there's a quiet satisfaction in it.
- His bedroom is tidy. Not fanatically so, but in the way that suggests he finds mess genuinely stressful. His desk has a desk tidy. His books are upright. There is a plant—a small cactus named Gerald—that he waters every Sunday.
- Plays five-a-side football on Saturday mornings, not because he loves it but because his dad wants him to and it gets him out of the house. He's not bad at it. He's not good either. He's reliable, which is the football equivalent of being "nice."
- Has a complicated relationship with his own competence. He knows he's clever, and he knows that being clever and anxious is an exhausting combination, and he sometimes resents that Leo gets to be funny and careless while he has to be careful and responsible.

**Trivial Details:**
- Eats toast with an irrational amount of butter. His mum once weighed the butter he put on a single slice: 28 grams. He was unapologetic.
- Has never seen *Hot Fuzz*, which Leo considers a personal failing.
- His phone case is plain black. He's considered getting a novelty one but can't decide, so he's had the plain black one for two years.
- Can do a perfect impression of their headteacher, Mr. Rudge, that he only does when he's sure no teachers are within earshot. It's note-perfect and slightly terrifying.
- Once helped Leo bury a dead bird in Leo's garden and said a few words over it ("It was probably a pigeon. It doesn't care. But fine."), which Leo has never forgotten, though neither of them has ever spoken about it again.

**Physicality:**
Shorter than Leo by a good four inches, and stocky—not fat, but solid, with the build of someone who eats well and moves regularly. He has a round face that makes him look younger than he is, close-cropped hair that his mum cuts, and dark brown skin that he's comfortable in. He carries himself with a stillness that can read as either calm or braced for impact—there's a tension in his posture, a readiness, as if his body is always half-prepared for something to go wrong.

When he's relaxed—and he's relaxed around Leo more than anyone—his face opens up. He smiles easily, and it transforms him, makes him look like the kid he actually is rather than the responsible adult he sometimes pretends to be. When he's anxious, he goes very still and very quiet, and his eyes fix on a middle distance, and you can almost see him running scenarios behind them.

He gestures minimally when he talks. One hand, mostly. A finger pointing, a palm upturned, a dismissive wave. His body language says "I'm here, I'm present, I'm not going to make a scene."

**Motive & Relationships:**
Moose's primary motive is **loyalty**. He doesn't care about the mystery—he thinks it's probably nothing, and he'd rather be doing literally anything else. But Leo cares, and Leo is his best friend, and that's enough. He follows Leo into the investigation not because he's curious but because he can't imagine not following. This loyalty is both his greatest strength and his biggest vulnerability, because it means he'll go along with things he knows are stupid, and he'll absorb damage that isn't his to absorb.

His secondary motive is **control**. The suspect list, the plans, the contingencies—these aren't just anxiety management. They're Moose's way of imposing order on a world that feels chaotic. The mystery threatens this order, and as it escalates, so does his need to manage it, which puts him in tension with Leo's chaotic approach.

With **Leo**, it's complicated. Moose loves Leo—platonically, fiercely, with the uncomplicated intensity of a sixteen-year-old boy who doesn't have the language for what this friendship means. But he's also aware that the friendship is slightly unequal. Leo talks, Moose listens. Leo performs, Moose is the audience. Moose doesn't mind, mostly, because he prefers listening, and because when Leo is funny, he's genuinely, brilliantly funny, and being around that energy is its own kind of joy. But sometimes—rarely, in quiet moments—Moose wonders what it would be like to have a friend who asked him how he was and waited for the answer.

With **his family**, it's love and mild suffocation. His parents are good people who want the best for him, and their expectations (good grades, good behaviour, good future) feel like a warm blanket that's occasionally too heavy. His sister Tia drives him up the wall, but he'd also fight anyone who hurt her.

**Flavour Dialogue / Internal Monologue:**

*Internal monologue, in the pump house:*
> The torch beam wobbled over concrete and rust and something that might have been moss or might have been mould, and Moose thought: *I am in a derelict building at half past eleven at night with my best friend, who thinks this is a film, and I am going to die here, and my mum will have to identify my body, and Tia will cry for exactly one day before she gets my room.*

*Dialogue, after the failed confrontation with Dan:*
> "So to be clear," Moose said, "we accused our friend of sending us a threatening text message, he didn't do it, and now he thinks we're paranoid weirdos."
> "He doesn't think we're paranoid weirdos."
> "He said, and I quote, 'You lot are actually mental.'"
> "That's just Dan being Dan."
> "That's Dan being *accurate*."

---

# Karen Finch

**Background & Personality:**
Karen is forty-two, Leo's mum, and she is doing her best. This is not a euphemism for "she's failing"—she's genuinely doing well, all things considered. She works part-time at the Wefton library (Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday mornings) and runs her Etsy shop, "Grove & Glow," from the kitchen table, making soy candles with names like "Forest Bathing," "Sunday Morning," and the bestseller, "F*cking Monday" (the asterisk is load-bearing; Etsy's content policy is a nightmare). The business does okay. Not great. Okay.

He should have gone to sleep. He should have closed his eyes and let the nothing-videos and the three blood drops dissolve into the usual soup of dreams that he never remembered. That's what a normal person would do. A normal person would think *weird text, probably a prank, go to sleep*.

Leo was not a normal person. Leo was a person who had watched too many films and played too many games and read too many threads on Reddit about unexplained phenomena, and his brain was now running scenarios at a speed that made sleep impossible.

What if it was someone who knew him? Someone with his number, someone who'd chosen *him*, specifically, to receive three blood drops at midnight. That was targeted. That was personal. That was—

He could reply. He could type "who is this" and send it and wait. He could type something funny, something deflecting, something that turned the whole thing into a joke so he could control it. He could—

The question mark sat in the dark, glowing faintly on a screen he couldn't see, in a message he hadn't answered, from a person he didn't know.

Leo closed his eyes.

Sleep came slowly, and when it came, it was thin and restless, full of half-formed images—canals in the dark, the sound of water, a door that was slightly open when it should have been closed. In the morning, he'd tell himself it was nothing. He'd laugh about it with Moose. He'd come up with a plan to prank Dan that was elaborate and pointless and would probably backfire.

But right now, in the dark, with the question mark still glowing and the lavender still rising and the hall light still on, Leo lay very still and listened to his own breathing and thought:

*What if it's not Dan?*

# Chapter 2: The Revenge

Dan Kowalski was sitting in the canteen, eating a sausage roll, and looking exactly like someone who had never sent a blood-drop emoji in his life.

"You sent us a text last night," Leo said, sliding into the seat opposite. Moose dropped into the seat beside him with the cautious precision of a man sitting down on a bench he suspected was wet.

"What?" Dan said, through sausage roll.

"Last night. Just after midnight. Three blood drops. Don't play innocent."

Dan chewed. Swallowed. Looked from Leo to Moose and back again with the calm, slightly confused expression of a golden retriever who'd been accused of tax fraud.

"I didn't send you anything last night. I was asleep. Like a normal person."

"We checked," Moose said. "The message came from an unknown number, but we thought—"

"You thought I'd buy a burner phone to send you blood emojis?" Dan set down his sausage roll. He looked genuinely offended, which was inconvenient, because Leo had been counting on Dan finding it funny. Offended Dan was harder to manage than amused Dan. Offended Dan had *feelings*.

"Not a burner phone," Leo said, though he hadn't ruled it out. "Maybe you used someone else's phone. Maybe—"

"Leo." Dan's voice was flat. "Why would I send you blood emojis?"

"For a laugh."

"What's funny about blood emojis?"

"I don't know yet. That's why it's a mystery."

Dan looked at Moose again. "Is he always like this?"

"More or less," Moose said.

"Show me your phone," Leo said.

Dan stared at him.

"Just—show me. Let me see your sent messages."

"This is insane."

"Just show me."

Dan sighed the sigh of a man who knows he's innocent but also knows that innocence is not a defence against his friends' paranoia. He unlocked his phone, opened his messages, and handed it over with the resigned air of someone submitting to a police search.

Leo scrolled. He scrolled through Dan's sent messages with the intensity of a forensic analyst, examining timestamps, recipients, content. There were texts to his mum about dinner, texts to a girl named Anika that were mostly emojis (none of them blood), and a text to a group chat called "Wolves lol" that contained a single message: "we are so back."

No blood drops. No unknown numbers. Nothing.

Leo handed the phone back.

"Huh," he said.

"Huh," Dan repeated. "Can I have my sausage roll back?"

"You never lost your sausage roll."

"I lost my appetite. That's worse."

The three of them sat in silence for a moment. Around them, the canteen hummed with the usual lunchtime chaos—someone shouting about a lost bag, the clatter of trays, the specific frequency of thirty teenagers all talking at the same volume. Through the windows, the sky was the colour of a wet flannel, which was the default colour of the sky in Wefton from October to April.

"So if it wasn't Dan," Moose said carefully, "who was it?"

"I don't know," Leo said. And then, because admitting uncertainty felt like failure: "But someone sent it. And someone's going to pay."

"Pay how?" Dan asked.

"I haven't figured that out yet."

"Brilliant."

The plan, when it came, was not brilliant. It was the opposite of brilliant. It was the kind of plan that a sixteen-year-old boy devises at lunchtime on three hours' sleep and a vague sense of injustice, and it had all the strategic coherence of a cat falling off a counter.

They would send something back. Something scary. Something that would make the unknown number think twice before sending cryptic messages to strangers in the middle of the night.

The question was: what?

"A clown," Leo said.

"A clown," Moose repeated.

"Everyone's scared of clowns."

"I'm not scared of clowns," Dan said.

"You're scared of other things."

"Like what?"

"Irrelevance," Leo said, and Dan threw a chip at him.

They settled on a photo. Leo had one saved on his phone—a still from a film he'd watched last Halloween, of a clown standing in a doorway, backlit, face in shadow. It was genuinely unsettling, in the way that any image can be unsettling if you stare at it long enough and you're already primed for weirdness.

"Send it," Moose said, though his voice had the tone of a man watching someone step onto a rollercoaster he'd already decided not to ride.

Leo sent it.

They waited.

The canteen cleared around them. The lunch bell rang. They didn't move. They sat at the table with their phones out, watching the screens with the focused intensity of bomb disposal experts, waiting for a response.

Five minutes. Ten. The canteen was empty now except for a cleaner who was mopping around them with the pointed patience of someone who'd like them to leave.

Then: a single character. A question mark.

?

"That's it?" Leo said.

"That's it," Moose confirmed.

"Maybe they're scared."

"Maybe they're confused. We sent them a clown."

"Scared and confused. That's good."

Then, five minutes later, while Leo was still composing a triumphant message about psychological warfare, a new message came through. Not text. An image.

It loaded slowly—the canteen Wi-Fi was never good and was especially bad in the afternoons, when every phone in the building was fighting for bandwidth like starved dogs at a bowl. The image pixelated, sharpened, resolved.

It was a photograph of their school. The front entrance, specifically—the concrete canopy, the automatic doors, the sign that read WEFTON HIGH in letters that were supposed to look modern but instead looked like a ransom note written by an architect. The photo had been taken from the car park, near the bike sheds, at an angle that meant the photographer had been standing approximately where Leo and Moose had been standing at lunch.

Leo looked up from his phone. Through the canteen window, he could see the car park. The bike sheds. The exact spot.

"When was this taken?" Moose asked. His voice was different now—quieter, tighter, the voice he used when his anxiety was spiking and he was trying very hard to sound normal.

"Today," Leo said. "Look at the sky. That's today's sky."

They stared at the photo. They stared at the car park. They stared at each other.

"So," Moose said. "Someone was watching us."

"Looks like it."

"At lunch."

"Yep."

"While we were planning to send them a clown."

"Also yep."

Moose closed his eyes. He did this sometimes when the world was too much—just shut down the visual input and exist in the dark for a second, recalibrating. When he opened them, his face was calm in the way that a lake is calm before someone throws a rock into it.

"Right," he said. "So we've gone from 'it's probably Dan being edgy' to 'someone was photographing us from the car park.' That's an escalation."

"It's not an escalation. It's a response. We sent them a clown. They sent us context."

"That's not context. That's a *threat*."

"It's a photo of a school."

"A photo of *our* school. Taken from *our* car park. On the same day we sent them a threatening image. That's not context, Leo. That's someone saying 'I know where you are.'"

He wanted to say all of these things because saying them would make the situation feel manageable, and manageable was what he needed it to be.

"Okay," he said. "So it's not Dan."

"It's not Dan."

"And someone's watching us."

"Someone took a photo of the school from where we were standing."

"Which is basically the same thing."

"It's not basically the same thing."

" Moose. Focus."

Moose focused. He took a breath. He pulled out his phone and opened his notes app, and Leo watched him create a new note titled "INVESTIGATION" in capital letters, and beneath it, the first entry:

> Suspect 1: Unknown.
> Method: burner phone.
> Status: they know our location.
> Confidence: n/a.

"It's a start," Moose said.

"It's a list with one entry."

"Every list starts with one entry."

"Not every list. Shopping lists start with—"

"Leo."

"Right. Yeah. One entry. Good start."

They left the canteen. The cleaner watched them go with the expression of a woman who had seen sixteen-year-olds do stupider things than leave a canteen in slow motion, and who was tired of all of it.

Walking back to class, Leo felt it—that buzz, that electric hum that comes when something shifts from "probably nothing" to "maybe something," when the world stops being a flat, grey surface and develops texture, and depth, and the faintest suggestion of a plot.

This was interesting.

This was, against all probability and common sense, actually interesting.

He caught Moose's eye and grinned, and Moose didn't grin back, because Moose was thinking about the photo and the car park and the angle and the fact that someone had been standing where they'd been standing, watching them, and none of it was funny.

But Leo was grinning. Because this was the bit in the film where it gets good.

# Chapter 3: The List

Leo's bedroom smelled like old toast and the ghost of Karen's latest candle—"Sunday Morning," which smelled like linen and something floral that Leo couldn't identify and didn't want to ask about because then his mum would explain the difference between bergamot and neroli, and he'd have to stand there and pretend to care about essential oils for five minutes while his actual life was happening.

Moose was sitting on the floor with his back against the bed, phone in hand, thumb moving with the methodical precision of a man filing a tax return. On the screen was his notes app, the "INVESTIGATION" note now expanded to fill half a page, colour-coded in a system that Leo found both impressive and mildly unhinged.

"Right," Moose said. "Who do we know who has our numbers, knows where we go to school, and would think blood-drop emojis are an appropriate form of communication?"

"Everyone in Year 11," Leo said.

"More specific."

Leo paced. His room was too small for pacing—three steps one way, three steps back—but he did it anyway because pacing made him feel like a detective in a film, and feeling like a detective was more fun than actually investigating, which involved sitting on floors and making lists.

"Okay. Ellis Park."

"The new kid?"

"He wears black. He keeps to himself. He once drew a weird symbol in his maths book."

"What kind of symbol?"

"I don't know. A weird one."

"It was a Rubik's cube, Leo. Priya told me. She sits next to him."

"A Rubik's cube *could* be a sigil."

"It's a toy. It's a children's toy shaped like a cube."

"In the right context—"

"There is no right context in which a Rubik's cube is a sigil."

Leo stopped pacing. "Fine. What about Mrs. Barker?"

"Mrs. Barker," Moose repeated, in the flat tone of a man who has been asked to consider something he has already considered and rejected.

"She confiscated your phone."

"In Year 9."

"With *malice*."

"She confiscated it because I was playing Subway Surfers in double maths. That's not malice. That's pedagogy."

"She looked at me when she did it."

"She looks at everyone. She has eyes."

"She looked at me with *meaning*."

"Leo." Moose looked up from his phone. "Mrs. Barker is forty-seven years old. She drives a Volvo. She has a cat named Bismarck. She is not sending us blood emojis."

"You don't know that."

"I know that she's a history teacher with a cat named Bismarck. That's enough."

Leo sat down on the bed. The springs complained. Everything in this room was old—the bed, the desk, the curtains that his mum had bought from Dunelm in 2019 and which had faded from navy to a colour that was technically blue but spiritually grey. He picked at a thread on the duvet cover and thought about suspects.

"Priya," he said.

Moose stopped typing. "Priya."

"She said my haircut was interesting."

"When?"

"Year 10."

"Leo, that was a compliment."

"It was *loaded*."

"It was about your hair."

"People say things about your hair when they can't say things about your character. It's a deflection."

"Or it's a compliment about your hair."

"She could be behind this."

"Priya Mehta, who is in the top set for everything and volunteers at the Wefton Animal Shelter on weekends, is sending us blood-drop emojis because she said your haircut was interesting in Year 10."

"When you say it like that—"

"It sounds insane. Because it is."

The door opened. Karen appeared in the gap, holding two mugs and wearing the expression of a woman who has brought offerings and hopes they will be accepted.

"Tea," she said. "And I made those little breadsticks you like. The ones with the—"

"Thanks, Mum."

"—cheese on. They're in the kitchen. Just help yourselves." She hovered. She was good at hovering—there was a specific Karen hover that occupied the precise boundary between "I'm respecting your privacy" and "I would very much like to know what you're doing." Her eyes moved from Leo to Moose to the phone in Moose's hand and back again.

"You two collaborating on something?"

"Homework," Leo said.

"History," Moose added, because Moose was a better liar than Leo, which was ironic because Leo was the one who thought of himself as the creative one.

"History! Lovely. What period?"

"The... recent one," Leo said.

"Well, that's good. You know, your dad—" She stopped. The word "dad" had left her mouth before she could catch it, and now it was in the room, sitting on the bed between them like an unwanted guest. Karen's face did a complicated thing—apologetic, annoyed at herself, determined to push through.

"—your dad always said history was important. Anyway. Breadsticks. Kitchen. Love you."

She closed the door. The silence she left behind was the specific silence that follows a parent accidentally mentioning the other parent—loaded, uncomfortable, briefly acknowledged by everyone present before being deliberately ignored.

"She's nice," Moose said, after a moment.

"She's a lot," Leo said, but there was no venom in it. He loved his mum. He was embarrassed by her. These were not contradictory states; they were the twin engines of being sixteen.

He got up and retrieved the breadsticks. They were, objectively, excellent—crispy, cheesy, the kind of snack that fills a hole without requiring commitment. He brought the plate back and set it between them, and they ate in the focused, wordless way of teenage boys encountering free food.

"Right," Moose said, brushing crumbs from his phone. "I've got the list."

He turned the screen so Leo could see. The note was now a proper document:

**INVESTIGATION - SUSPECT LIST**

> **Ellis Park** (new kid, black coat, "weird symbol" = Rubik's cube)
> Confidence: LOW
> Reason for suspicion: general vibe
> Reason against: it's a Rubik's cube

> **Mrs. Barker** (history teacher, confiscated phone)
> Confidence: VERY LOW
> Reason for suspicion: Leo's feelings
> Reason against: she's a teacher with a cat

> **Priya Mehta** (said haircut was "interesting")
> Confidence: ZERO
> Reason for suspicion: none
> Reason against: all of them

> **Unknown** (burner phone, knows our location)
> Confidence: UNKNOWN
> Reason for suspicion: they sent the text and took a photo
> Reason against: we don't know who they are, which is the whole problem

"Four suspects," Leo said.

"Three of whom are innocent and one of whom we can't identify."

"That's a start."

"It's a list of people who haven't done anything."

"Every investigation starts somewhere."

"Most investigations start with evidence. We started with a vibe."

Leo took a breadstick. Crunched it thoughtfully. "The unknown is the interesting one."

"The unknown is the only one with actual evidence against them."

"Exactly. So we focus on the unknown."

"How? We don't know who they are."

"We know they have a burner phone. We know they were at the school today. We know they responded to our clown with a question mark, which means they're either confused or unimpressed, and both of those are data points."

Moose stared at him. "You just said 'data points' like you know what that means."

"I know what it means."

"You got a C in statistics."

"A C is a pass."

"A C is a polite fail."

"The point is," Leo said, "we have more information than we think. The phone number. The location. The timing. It's not nothing."

"It's not much."

"It's enough to keep going."

Moose looked at the list again. He scrolled up, scrolled down, as if the answer might be hiding in the whitespace between entries. Then he locked his phone and put it in his pocket, and the screen went dark, and the list disappeared, and they were just two boys in a bedroom with breadsticks and no answers.

"Okay," Moose said. "We keep going."

"Yeah?"

"Yeah. But if we end up in a canal, I'm blaming you."

"That's fair."

They finished the breadsticks. Karen had made too many, as she always did, because Karen expressed love through overcatering, and the evidence of this—the plate, the crumbs, the faint smell of cheese—lingered in the room like a warm, slightly embarrassing hug.

Outside, the sky darkened toward evening. The rain started again, because the rain always started again in Wefton, tapping against the window in a rhythm that was either soothing or maddening depending on your mood, and Leo's mood was neither soothing nor maddening but something in between—the restless, electric feeling of being on the edge of something, even if that something was probably nothing.

His phone buzzed.

He grabbed it. Not the unknown number. Not Moose. Not Dan. Just a notification from his mum's Etsy shop: "Grove & Glow: New Listing! 'Forest Bathing' - Cedar & Eucalyptus - £12.99."

He put the phone down.

"Tomorrow," he said.

"Tomorrow," Moose agreed.

And in the quiet of Leo's room, with the rain and the toast-smell and the ghost of neroli, the investigation rested. Not solved. Not abandoned. Just paused, like a film at intermission, waiting for the next act.

The unknown number sat in Leo's phone like a stone in a shoe—present, uncomfortable, impossible to ignore. And on Moose's phone, the list grew, entry by entry, suspect by suspect, colour-coded and organized, a tiny monument to the belief that if you just arrange the data correctly, the world will make sense.

It won't. But they're sixteen, and they don't know that yet.

# Chapter 4: Suspect Zero

Ellis Park lived above the Co-op. Leo knew this because he'd overheard someone say it in registration, and he'd stored it away in the part of his brain that labelled people as "information to be filed under potential threats," which was a section that had been mostly empty until this week and was now dangerously overactive.

They followed him after school.

This was not, Leo would later reflect, one of his better ideas. It wasn't even one of his mediocre ideas. It was an idea that existed in the negative space below mediocre—a void of judgment so complete that future Leo would look back on it with the kind of cringing, full-body shame usually reserved for remembering song lyrics you used to sing with conviction.

But present Leo, the Leo of the moment, thought it was genius.

"We're not following him," Leo whispered, from behind a bin at the edge of the school car park. "We're conducting discreet surveillance."

"We're following him," Moose said, from behind the same bin, pressed against Leo's shoulder in a way that was both intimate and deeply uncomfortable. "And he's buying a birthday card."

This was true. Ellis Park, suspect zero, the boy in the black coat who Leo had decided was responsible for the blood-drop emojis based on absolutely nothing, was currently standing in the Card Factory at the Wefton retail park, holding a birthday card with a cartoon dog on the front and reading the message inside with the concentrated expression of someone choosing a card that actually means something.

They'd tailed him from school. It had taken forty minutes. Ellis had walked to the bus stop, waited eleven minutes (Moose counted), taken the bus two stops to the retail park, and entered the Card Factory with the purposeful stride of someone on a mission. Leo had narrated the entire journey in a hushed, breathless whisper that made everything sound more significant than it was.

"He's heading north."

"He's walking to the bus stop."

"He's waiting for the bus. This is suspicious."

"Waiting for a bus is not suspicious. It's public transport."

"He's getting on the bus."

"Because he's going somewhere."

"But *where*?"

"Probably somewhere normal."

"Or somewhere sinister."

"Leo, he's going to the retail park. The retail park has a Card Factory and a Costa and a Pets at Home. There's nothing sinister there."

"There's a Smyths Toys."

"What's sinister about Smyths Toys?"

"I don't know yet. But I'm keeping an eye on it."

Now they were crouched behind a metal bin at the edge of the retail park car park, watching Ellis through the Card Factory window, and Leo was starting to feel the first, faint stirrings of doubt. Not because the surveillance was going badly—it was going exactly as planned, in the sense that they were surveilling and Ellis was being surveilled—but because the reality of Ellis Park was not matching the profile Leo had constructed in his head.

The profile: a mysterious new kid, possibly a goth, definitely sending blood emojis, potentially dangerous, almost certainly harbouring dark secrets.

The reality: a sixteen-year-old boy buying a birthday card.

Ellis came out of the Card Factory. He held the card carefully, both hands, as if it were something fragile. He walked to the bus stop and sat down on the bench. The bench was empty. The sky was the grey-wet colour that was Wefton's default, and the rain had started again—light, persistent, the kind that doesn't soak you but dampens everything, making the world feel slightly defeated.

Ellis sat there. Alone. Holding a birthday card against his chest to keep it dry.

And something shifted in Leo.

It wasn't a dramatic shift—not a revelation, not an epiphany, not the moment where the soundtrack swells and the protagonist suddenly understands the meaning of life. It was smaller than that. Quieter. A flicker of recognition that passed through him like a draft under a door.

He knew what that looked like. That specific posture—shoulders hunched, head slightly down, the careful stillness of a person who has learned to make themselves small in public spaces. He'd done it himself, at twelve, sitting on the kerb outside his dad's new place in Telford, waiting for a lift that was always twenty minutes late and sometimes didn't come at all. The birthday card was different from a kerb, but the loneliness was the same—the same colour, the same weight, the same quiet resignation of a person who is alone and knows it and is managing.

Leo said nothing.

Moose, beside him, was quiet too. Maybe he saw it. Maybe he just sensed the shift in Leo, the way you sense a change in air pressure before a storm. Either way, he didn't speak.

They watched Ellis wait for the bus. It came after seven minutes. He got on. The bus pulled away, and the bench was empty, and the rain kept falling on the spot where he'd been sitting, and the whole thing was so profoundly ordinary that Leo felt something he couldn't name—a tightness in his chest that wasn't anxiety or excitement but something worse: shame.

He'd followed a kid to a Card Factory. He'd crouched behind a bin. He'd built a narrative in which this kid—this specific, real kid with a birthday card and a black coat and a quiet way of sitting—was a villain, a suspect, a character in Leo's story. And the kid was just a kid. Just a boy buying a card for someone, sitting alone in the rain, going home to whatever was waiting for him above the Co-op.

"Leo?" Moose's voice was careful. "You okay?"

"Yeah," Leo said. His voice sounded wrong—too quiet, too flat. Not his voice at all. "Yeah, I'm fine."

"Because you've gone weird."

"I'm not weird. I'm thinking."

"You're thinking in a weird way."

"What does thinking in a weird way look like?"

"Like that. Like you're doing now. With the face."

Leo didn't answer. He was still looking at the empty bench. The rain was filling the space where Ellis had been sitting, puddling on the plastic seat, running off the edges in small, constant streams that caught the light from the streetlamp and held it for a second before letting it go.

"We should go," he said.

"Yeah," Moose agreed.

They walked to the bus stop. They didn't speak on the bus. They didn't speak walking from the bus stop to Leo's street, where their paths diverged—Moose left, Leo right, the same split they'd made a thousand times before, the geometry of a friendship measured in which way you turn at the junction.

At home, Karen was in the kitchen, making candles. The house smelled of cedar and something else—something warm and slightly sweet that Leo couldn't place. She looked up when he came in.

"Alright, love? Want some toast?"

"Yeah," he said. "Thanks."

He went upstairs. He sat on his bed. He pulled out his phone and opened the conversation with Moose, and his thumb hovered over the keyboard for a long time before he typed:

> maybe it's not ellis

Moose replied instantly:

> obviously

And then, a moment later:

> you alright?

Leo looked at the message. He thought about typing "fine," which was what he always typed, which was the default response, the one that closed conversations and maintained distance and kept everything safely on the surface where it couldn't hurt anyone.

He typed:

> yeah. just tired.

Moose:

> ok. night.

> night.

He put the phone down. The room was dark. The rain was still falling, tapping against the window in the same rhythm it had been tapping all day, and the house smelled of cedar and the ghost of lavender, and downstairs his mum was humming something tuneless while the wax melted, and Leo lay on his bed and stared at the ceiling and felt the shame settle into him like rain into soil—slow, quiet, soaking everything.

He should have felt stupid. He should have felt embarrassed. He'd followed an innocent kid to a Card Factory and watched him buy a birthday card, and the whole thing was ridiculous and he should be laughing about it.

But he wasn't laughing. He was thinking about a boy on a bench, holding a card against the rain, and the specific, inarguable loneliness of that image, and how easy it was to turn a person into a suspect when you weren't looking at them properly.

He closed his eyes.

In the dark, the shame didn't go away. It just settled, becoming part of the room, part of the night, part of the quiet, steady rhythm of the rain on the glass. And somewhere in the space between waking and sleeping, Leo thought—not for the first time, but for the first time with clarity—that maybe the problem wasn't the mystery.

Maybe the problem was the detective.

# Chapter 5: The Pump House

The text came at 9:47pm. A location pin, dropped into the conversation with the casual precision of a brick through a window. No words. No explanation. Just a map fragment showing a spot by the canal—the Victorian pump house, the one everyone knew about and no one went near, the one with the boarded windows and the roof that sagged like a tired horse.

Moose's reply was immediate:

> absolutely not

Leo:
> we have to go

Moose:
> we absolutely do not have to go

Leo:
> someone sent us a location. that's an invitation.

Moose:
> that's a lure. there's a difference.

Leo:
> come on

Moose:
> no

Leo:
> please

Moose:
> no

Leo:
> I'll buy you chips after

A pause. The typing indicator appeared, vanished, appeared again. Moose was weighing the value of his personal safety against the value of free chips, and the chips were winning, because the chips were from Dave's and Dave's chips were the best in Wefton and possibly the Midlands, and Moose was a pragmatist.

Moose:
> dave's chips

Leo:
> dave's chips

Moose:
> large

Leo:
> large with curry sauce

Moose:
> fine. but if we die I'm haunting you first.

They met at the canal bridge at half past ten. The night was cold—properly cold, the kind of cold that finds the gaps in your clothes and settles in, making itself at home. The canal was black and still, reflecting the streetlights in long, wobbly columns that looked like liquid gold but were just water and sodium and the optical illusion of being sixteen and standing somewhere you shouldn't be at half past ten on a school night.

The pump house sat fifty metres along the towpath, squat and dark against the sky. It had been built in the 1880s to manage water levels on the canal, and it had been abandoned in the 1970s, and since then it had served as a shelter for pigeons, a canvas for graffiti artists, and a source of urban legends that were mostly untrue but persistent—the ghost of a lock-keeper who'd drowned, the sound of machinery that no longer existed, the door that opened by itself on windy nights.

Leo had his phone torch on. The beam cut through the dark in a wobbly, unreliable cone that illuminated approximately three square feet of reality at a time—towpath, puddle, nettles, the concrete lip of the canal, which was closer than Leo liked.

"Stay away from the edge," Moose said.

"I am away from the edge."

"You're not. You're one step from the edge."

"I'm two steps."

"You're one and a half."

"Moose—"

"I don't want to have to tell your mum you drowned investigating a text message. She'd cry. I'd cry. It would be a whole thing."

They reached the pump house. Up close, it was larger than Leo remembered—two storeys of brick and iron, the windows boarded with plywood that was peeling and damp and covered in a layer of moss that looked like green velvet in the torchlight. The main door was a sheet of corrugated metal, slightly ajar, held in place by a padlock that was more rust than lock.

"Someone's been here recently," Moose said, pointing. The ground around the door was muddy, and in the mud were footprints—small, adult-sized, pressed into the wet earth with the clear definition of shoes that had been here within the last day.

"Could be anyone," Leo said, though his voice had lost its usual bounce. The pump house, in the dark, was not a film set. It was a real building, derelict and damp and smelling of rust and stagnant water, and the air around it was colder than the air on the towpath, as if the building was generating its own microclimate of discomfort.

They went in.

The interior was a single large room, the ceiling lost in shadow above them. Leo's torch swept across concrete floors, rusted machinery, the remains of a metal staircase that led to a mezzanine level that looked structurally unsound. The walls were covered in graffiti—tags, mostly, meaningless strings of letters in spray paint that had faded to pastels. The smell was complex: damp, rust, something organic that Leo didn't want to identify.

"Hello?" Leo called out, and immediately felt stupid, because who calls out "hello" in an abandoned pump house at half past ten at night? Only people in films. Only people who think their lives have soundtracks.

No answer. Just the drip of water somewhere unseen, steady and slow, like a clock made of liquid.

They moved deeper. The torch beam found the machinery first—massive iron wheels and gears, frozen in position, the ghosts of Victorian engineering that had once controlled the flow of water through the canal. They were impressive in the way that dead things can be impressive—monumental, silent, proof that something important had once happened here, even if no one remembered what.

Then the beam found the corner.

It was tucked behind the base of the staircase, in a space that was sheltered from the main room by a half-wall of brick. In the torchlight, it looked like a nest—arranged, deliberate, a pocket of domesticity in the industrial decay.

A sleeping bag. Dark blue, unzipped, the kind you buy from Go Outdoors for fifteen quid. On top of it, a pillow—a real pillow, not a bundled-up jacket, but an actual pillow with a pillowcase that had once been white and was now a colour Leo could only describe as "lived-in."

Next to the sleeping bag: a tin of beans, unopened. A plastic spoon. A torch—the cheap kind, yellow, that you get from petrol stations. A phone charger, coiled neatly. And, propped against the brick wall at the exact angle of something displayed with care, a drawing.

Leo crouched. He pointed the torch at the drawing and the light caught it and held it and wouldn't let go.

It was a child's drawing of a house. Crayon, on paper that had been torn from an exercise book. The house had a red door and a yellow window and a chimney with smoke coming out of it, and in front of the house were two stick figures—one tall, one small—holding hands. Above the house, in wobbly child's handwriting, the words:

**ME AND MUM**

Leo stared at it. The torch shook slightly in his hand—not much, just enough to make the drawing wobble on the wall, the stick figures swaying as if they were alive, as if they were walking, as if they were holding hands and walking away from the drawing and into the dark pump house where someone had been sleeping on the floor with a fifteen-quid sleeping bag and a tin of beans and a drawing of a home that wasn't here anymore.

He didn't say anything.

Moose, behind him, didn't say anything.

The silence was different now. It wasn't the comfortable silence of two friends who don't need to talk, or the charged silence of two boys in a scary place. It was the silence that comes when you've been playing a game and you suddenly realize it's not a game—that the things you've been treating as clues and suspects and plot points are actually lives, actually people, actually the specific, heartbreaking details of someone else's reality.

"Leo." Moose's voice was very quiet. "We should go."

"Yeah."

"Someone's sleeping here."

"Yeah."

"We should tell someone."

"Yeah."

They backed out of the corner. They walked through the main room, past the rusted machinery and the graffiti and the drip of water, and out through the corrugated metal door, and onto the towpath, and the night air hit them like a wall of cold that was somehow warmer than the inside of the pump house.

They walked along the canal in silence. The water was black and still. The streetlights cast their long, wobbly reflections. The towpath was muddy underfoot, and their shoes made sucking sounds with each step, and neither of them spoke, because there was nothing to say that wouldn't sound either too big or too small for what they'd seen.

At the bridge, where the towpath met the road, Leo stopped. He looked at Moose. Moose looked at him. In the sodium light, Moose's face was pale and serious, the anxiety not spiking but settling, becoming something quieter and more permanent—a knowledge, a weight.

"We'll tell someone," Leo said.

"Who?"

"I don't know. The school. The council. Someone."

"When?"

"Tomorrow."

Moose nodded. Then he said, very quietly, almost inaudibly under the sound of the water and the distant traffic and the wind in the trees:

"What if they're still there?"

Leo didn't answer. He didn't have an answer. The question hung between them in the cold air, and the cold air held it, and the night held it, and the black canal reflected nothing, because the canal doesn't care about sixteen-year-old boys and their mysteries and their sudden, sickening realization that the world is bigger and sadder and more complicated than they'd allowed themselves to believe.

They walked to Dave's. They ordered chips—large, with curry sauce—and sat in the fluorescent-lit warmth of the café, surrounded by the smell of vinegar and the sound of Sandra wiping down tables, and they ate without talking, and the chips were good and the curry sauce was hot and the café was bright and safe and completely unable to erase the image of a child's drawing of a house with a red door and a yellow window and two stick figures holding hands.

After, walking home, Leo said: "We'll figure it out."

And Moose said: "Okay."

And neither of them believed it, but they said it anyway, because sometimes saying something is the only tool you have, even when the thing you're saying is a lie wrapped in the shape of a promise.

At home, Karen was asleep. The house was dark and quiet and smelled of nothing. Leo went to his room and sat on his bed and looked at his phone and saw the location pin still sitting in the conversation, a little red dot on a little map, pointing at a place that was real, that was dark, that was cold, where someone was maybe sleeping right now, or maybe not, and he didn't know which was worse.

He didn't sleep. Not for a long time. And when he did, he dreamed of stick figures walking through dark buildings, holding hands, looking for a door that was red and a window that was yellow and a chimney with smoke, and finding nothing but concrete and rust and the steady, patient drip of water in the dark.

In the morning, he'd think about what to do. In the morning, he'd make a plan.

But right now, in the dark, with the rain and the silence and the weight of something he couldn't carry and couldn't put down, Leo lay still and listened to the house breathe and thought about a drawing of a house that was just a drawing, and a home that was just a memory, and a boy who might be sleeping in a pump house by the canal, and he didn't know the boy's name, and he didn't know the boy's story, and he didn't know how to help, and the not-knowing was the worst part of all.

# Chapter 6: The Dracula

The next text arrived at 3:14pm, which was both oddly specific and deeply inconvenient because Leo was in the middle of double maths and his phone was in his bag and Mrs. Barker was circling the room with the predatory patience of a woman who knew exactly which students had devices on their person and was waiting for one to vibrate.

It buzzed twice. Then stopped. Then buzzed again.

Leo caught Moose's eye across the classroom. Moose gave a tiny, almost imperceptible shake of his head—the universal signal for "do not check your phone, she will confiscate it, and then where will we be." Leo responded with a tiny, almost imperceptible shrug—the universal signal for "I know, but I want to."

The lesson ended at 3:30. Leo had his phone out before the bell finished ringing.

The unknown number:

> DRAMA STUDIO. 6PM. COME ALONE.

Leo showed it to Moose in the corridor. Moose read it twice, his face cycling through a series of expressions—skepticism, concern, a brief flicker of something that might have been excitement before the anxiety smothered it.

"'Come alone,'" Moose read aloud. "That's from a film."

"Every line is from a film if you think about it hard enough."

"No one says 'come alone' in real life. That's a screenwriter's line."

"Maybe they're a screenwriter."

"We're not being lured to the drama studio by a screenwriter."

"We're not being lured at all. It's an invitation."

"A summons."

"Same thing."

"It's really not."

But they went. Of course they went. Because the pump house had changed something—not in the mystery, which was still unresolved, but in them, in the way they related to the unknown. Before the pump house, the investigation was a game—a way to kill time, a reason to text each other at midnight, a shared fiction that made Wefton slightly less grey. After the pump house, it was something else. Someone was sleeping rough. Someone had left a drawing of a house propped against a wall. And the unknown number was connected to it, somehow, in a way they didn't understand but couldn't ignore.

So they went.

They arrived at the drama studio at ten to six. The school was mostly empty—the after-school clubs had finished, the staff car park was down to three cars, and the corridors were lit by every third fluorescent tube, casting everything in a sickly yellow that made the school look like a hospital in a horror film.

The drama studio was at the end of the arts corridor, behind a fire door that had a sign reading NO FOOD OR DRINK BEYOND THIS POINT, which someone had amended with a biro to read NO FOOD OR DRINK BEYOND THIS PORK, which had been there since Year 9 and which no teacher had ever bothered to correct.

They pushed through the fire door. The drama studio was large—a converted gymnasium with a sprung floor and blackout curtains and a lighting rig that hadn't worked properly since 2017. It smelled of dust and old paint and the particular mustiness of a room that was used by teenagers who sweated and shouted and occasionally threw things.

The lights were on.

Not the overheads—the stage lights. Red and blue, casting the room in a lurid, theatrical glow that turned the ordinary space into something that looked like a nightclub had crashed into a church. In the centre of the room, on a makeshift stage assembled from drama blocks and determination, stood approximately fifteen students in various states of costume.

Leo recognized most of them. There was Becca Hart, the head of the Drama Society, who wore a velvet cape and an expression of supreme self-importance. There was Tom Chen, who was dressed as a vampire but looked more like a man who'd lost a fight with a red marker. There was Fatima Noor, who was reading from a script with the intensity of someone performing Shakespeare at the Globe rather than rehearsing a school play in a converted gymnasium in Wefton.

They were rehearsing a play.

The play, as Leo would learn in the next seven minutes, was called *Blood and Shadows: A Retelling of Dracula for the Modern Age*, and it was written, directed, and starring Becca Hart, who had described it in the school newsletter as "a bold reimagining of Stoker's masterpiece that interrogates the intersection of power, desire, and the monstrous feminine."

It was, by any objective measure, terrible.

"What," Moose said, from the doorway.

"Oh good, an audience," Becca said, not looking up from the stage. "Stay. We need the feedback."

"We're not—"

"Shh. We're at a crucial moment. Tom, you're not being menacing enough. You need to *be* the night."

"I am being the night," Tom said, in a voice that was trying for Transylvanian and landing somewhere near Slough.

"You're being the evening. At best, you're being dusk. I need *night*. I need *midnight*. I need—"

"Becca," Leo said. "Why did you send us a location pin to the drama studio?"

Becca looked at him. She had the expression of someone who has been interrupted during a sacred ritual and is deciding whether to forgive the interruption or sacrifice the interrupter to the gods of theatre.

"I didn't send you anything. We're rehearsing. We rehearse every Tuesday and Thursday from five to eight. It's on the noticeboard. It's been on the noticeboard since September."

"The text said 'come alone.'"

"I don't know anything about a text. Tom, *more cape*."

Tom swished his cape with more commitment.

"We thought—" Moose began.

"You thought what? That someone lured you to the drama studio? For what purpose? To witness our art?"

"To be fair," Leo said, "your art involves blood."

"Of course it involves blood. It's Dracula. Dracula involves blood. Blood is central to the text. The blood-drop emojis are part of our promotional campaign." She pulled out her phone and showed them the Drama Society's Instagram page. The most recent post was a graphic of three blood-drop emojis above the words BLOOD AND SHADOWS - COMING SOON - WEFTON HIGH DRAMA STUDIO. It had seventeen likes.

"Those are the same emojis," Moose said, staring at the screen.

"Obviously. They're emojis. There's a limited palette. You use them or you don't."

"But—"

"We've been putting them everywhere. Posters. Flyers. The toilet doors. We even projected them onto the side of the science block last week, but Mr. Henderson made us stop because he said it was 'unsettling,' which, honestly, is the best review we've ever received."

Leo stared at the Instagram post. He stared at the three blood drops. He stared at the caption: *The night is coming. Are you ready?*

"So the emojis," he said slowly. "They're for your play."

"They're for the *marketing* of our play. The emojis represent the blood that is central to Dracula's mythology. They symbolise—"

"I understand what they symbolise."

"Good. Auditions are next week if you're interested. We need more bodies. Literally, for the crowd scenes. Metaphorically, for the ensemble."

Leo looked at Moose. Moose looked at Leo. Something was happening behind their eyes—a recalibration, a reprocessing, a rapid reassessment of everything they thought they knew. The blood drops were from the Drama Society. The blood drops were marketing. The blood drops were—

Wait.

"The Instagram post," Leo said. "When was it posted?"

"Three weeks ago."

"And the emojis have been on posters since when?"

"September."

"But we got the text last Tuesday. At midnight."

"So?"

"So if your campaign started in September, why did we get the text last week?"

Becca's expression shifted. The supreme self-importance flickered, replaced by something more uncertain—a crack in the performance, a moment of genuine confusion that she covered almost immediately with a return to theatrical authority.

"I don't know. Maybe someone forwarded it. Maybe it went viral."

"A school play marketing campaign went viral?"

"It could happen. We have seventeen likes."

"You have seventeen likes."

"Seventeen is a start."

Moose stepped forward. His voice was quiet, measured, the voice he used when he was thinking clearly and wanted everyone else to think clearly too.

"Becca. Did anyone from the Drama Society text us those emojis? Personally? From a phone?"

"No. We use the Instagram. We use the posters. We don't text individual students. That would be weird."

"It would be weird," Leo agreed.

"Although," Becca added, "now that you mention it, someone did ask about the emojis last week. In the group chat."

Leo's attention sharpened. "Who?"

"One of the Year 9s. They help with set design. They said they thought the emojis were 'cool' and asked if they could 'use them for something.' I said sure, because I'm generous with intellectual property."

"Which Year 9?"

"I don't remember. One of the small ones."

"That doesn't narrow it down."

"They're all small. They're Year 9."

Moose was already on his phone, scrolling through the Drama Society's Instagram, looking for the comment, the name, the thread. Leo watched him—watched the focus, the methodical precision, the way Moose's thumb moved with purpose through the digital noise—and felt something shift again. The mystery wasn't solved. The mystery had just gotten more complicated, and more mundane, and somehow, in its mundanity, more real.

The blood drops were marketing.

Someone had borrowed the marketing.

And that someone had texted Leo and Moose at midnight, and then sent a photo of the school, and then a location pin for the pump house, and none of it was connected to Dracula or Becca Hart or the terrible play that Tom Chen was performing with all the menace of a damp towel.

They left the drama studio. The sounds of rehearsal followed them down the corridor—Tom's Transylvanian-that-was-really-Slough, Becca's directorial barking, the thud of drama blocks being rearranged. The fire door closed behind them, and the corridor was quiet, and the school was empty, and the fluorescent lights buzzed overhead in the sickly yellow that made everything look like a photograph of itself.

"Right," Moose said, in the car park. "So it's not the Drama Society."

"It's a Year 9 who borrowed the emojis."

"We're being haunted by a Year 9."

"We're not being haunted."

"We're being texted by someone in Year 9 who has a burner phone, took a photo of our school, and sent us a location pin to an abandoned pump house where someone is sleeping rough. That's either haunting or stalking, and I'm not sure which is worse."

"Or," Leo said, "it's something else entirely."

"Like what?"

"Like we've been looking at this wrong the whole time."

Moose looked at him. The car park was dark and the sky was the colour of nothing and the school behind them was a concrete block of empty classrooms and buzzing lights, and in the drama studio a boy dressed as a vampire was trying and failing to be the night, and somewhere in Wefton a Year 9 with a burner phone was doing something that none of them understood.

"Okay," Moose said. "So what do we do?"

"We find the Year 9."

"How? We don't even know their name."

"We know they're in Year 9. We know they asked about the emojis. We know they have a burner phone and they've been to the pump house. That's more than we had yesterday."

"It's barely more than we had yesterday."

"Barely more is still more."

They walked to Dave's. The chips were, as always, excellent. Sandra called them "love" and didn't ask why they looked like two boys who'd just discovered that their mystery was being conducted by a fourteen-year-old with access to emojis and poor judgment.

They ate in silence. The fluorescent lights hummed. The curry sauce was hot. The mystery was still there, sitting between them like a third person at the table, patient and unresolved, waiting for them to catch up.

And in the drama studio, Becca Hart stood on her stage and directed her terrible play and dreamed of seventeen likes becoming eighteen, and Tom Chen tried to be the night and became dusk at best, and somewhere in the dark of Wefton, a fourteen-year-old with a burner phone was doing something that was either a prank or a cry for help or both, and the answer was out there, in the rain, in the dark, in the space between the blood drops and the drawing of a house with a red door and two stick figures holding hands.

But not tonight. Tonight there were chips.

# Chapter 7: The Thing That Was Said

They found the Year 9 on Thursday.

His name was Callum Briggs. He was fourteen, small for his age, with hair the colour of wet sand and a face that was mostly freckles. He was in the bottom set for maths and the top set for drama, which seemed like an unlikely combination but wasn't—Callum had the kind of intelligence that was invisible in classrooms and blinding on a stage, and he'd volunteered for set design on Becca's Dracula play because it was the one place in the school where he made sense.

Moose found him. Of course Moose found him. Moose had spent two days methodically working through the Drama Society's group chat history, cross-referencing the emoji conversation with the Year 9 register, and identifying the student who'd asked to "use the emojis for something." It was meticulous, boring work—the digital equivalent of filing—and Moose had done it with the quiet, focused intensity that he brought to everything, the anxiety channeled into productivity, the need for control expressed as research.

"He's in 9C," Moose said, showing Leo his phone. "Form tutor is Mr. Phillips. He's got a younger sister in Year 7. His mum works at the Royal Shrewsbury Hospital."

"How do you know about his mum?"

"She's on the PTA email list. Karen's on it too. It's public information."

"You've been reading PTA emails."

"I've been *scanning* PTA emails. There's a difference."

They found Callum at lunch, sitting alone on the bench near the maths block—the same bench, Leo realized with a jolt, where Ellis Park sat. Apparently this bench was the designated spot for solitary fourteen-year-olds, a monument to the universal experience of eating your sandwiches alone and pretending you preferred it that way.

Callum looked up as they approached. His expression was wary—not scared, exactly, but braced, the way an animal looks when it hears a sound it doesn't recognize and is deciding whether to run or wait.

"Callum?" Leo said.

"Yeah?"

"We need to talk to you about some emojis."

Callum's face did something complicated. The wariness flickered, replaced by something else—a flash of guilt, maybe, or fear, or the particular panic of a fourteen-year-old who has done something he thought was funny and is now realizing it might have consequences.

"I don't know what you're talking about," he said, which was such an obvious lie that even Moose raised an eyebrow.

"The blood drops," Leo said. "You sent them to us."

"I didn't."

"Your phone—"

"I didn't send anything."

"Callum." Moose's voice was different now—gentler than Leo's, but with an edge of steel underneath, the voice of someone who has done the research and knows the facts and is offering you one chance to be honest before the facts do the talking for you. "We know you asked Becca about the emojis. We know you have a burner phone. We know you sent the location pin to the pump house. We know you took the photo of the school."

Callum stared at them. His freckles stood out against skin that had gone pale, and his hands were gripping the edge of the bench like he was trying to hold himself in place, and the sandwich in his lap was untouched, and Leo saw all of this—the freckles, the pale skin, the white knuckles—and felt the narrative in his head start to shift, the film-reel clicking, the story rearranging itself.

"Okay," Callum said. His voice was small. "Yeah. I sent the texts."

"Why?" Leo asked.

Callum didn't answer immediately. He looked at the canal, which was visible from the bench if you craned your neck—a strip of dark water between the school fence and the towpath. He looked at his sandwich. He looked at his hands. He was composing himself, Leo realized, gathering the scattered pieces of a story he hadn't planned to tell.

"My sister," he said finally. "She drew a picture. In Year 3. Of our house. With me and mum holding hands."

"The drawing in the pump house," Moose said quietly.

"Yeah. She drew it before—before everything. Before mum started working nights. Before dad left. Before we moved to the flat above the Co-op and she had to change schools and I had to—" He stopped. Swallowed. His throat moved in a way that was almost mechanical, a body forcing itself to function.

"I found the drawing in a box. In the new flat. And I thought—I thought if I put it somewhere, if I made it important, if I put it in a place where someone would *see* it—"

He stopped again. The bench was very quiet. The canal was very still. The sandwich sat in his lap like an offering to a god that wasn't listening.

"The pump house," Leo said.

"Yeah. I've been going there. After mum leaves for work. When Lily's asleep. It's—I don't know. It's somewhere that isn't the flat. Somewhere that's mine. I put the drawing there because I wanted it to be somewhere that mattered, and the flat doesn't feel like it matters, it just feels like a place where we're waiting for things to get better, and they're not getting better, they're just getting—" His voice cracked. Not dramatically, not with sobs, just a small fracture in the sound, like a bone that's been stressed too long and finally gives.

"And the texts?" Moose asked.

"I don't know. I found the burner phone in a charity shop. It was three quid. I thought—I thought if I sent something weird to someone, if I made something happen, then maybe I'd feel less—" He searched for the word. "—stuck. Like I was doing something. Like I was part of something. Even if it was just a prank. Even if it was just emojis."

He looked at Leo. His eyes were red but he wasn't crying. He was holding it together with the specific, practiced competence of a kid who has learned that falling apart is a luxury he can't afford.

"The photo of the school," Leo said. "Where were you standing?"

"In the car park. At lunch. I was watching you because I wanted to know if you'd gotten the text. I wanted to see if you were scared or confused or—something. I wanted to see that I'd made something happen."

"The location pin."

"I thought maybe if you came to the pump house you'd see the drawing and you'd—I don't know. Understand. That someone was going through something. That the emojis weren't just emojis."

Silence.

The canal reflected the sky, which was grey, which was always grey. A duck drifted past, oblivious. Somewhere in the school, a teacher shouted something that was absorbed by the concrete and came back as a muffled echo.

Leo opened his mouth to say something. He didn't know what. Something comforting, maybe, or something funny, because funny was what he did, funny was his default, funny was the tool he used to sand down the sharp edges of the world until they were smooth enough to touch.

But before he could speak, Moose spoke first.

"We should have told someone," Moose said. "About the pump house. After we went. We said we would, and we didn't."

It wasn't directed at Callum. It was directed at Leo. And it wasn't an accusation—not exactly—but it was close. It was the sound of a thing that had been sitting between them for two days, unspoken, and was now being spoken, and the speaking of it was worse than the silence because it made it real.

Leo felt something hot and uncomfortable move through his chest. "We were going to—"

"We said we'd tell someone. We went to the pump house and saw a sleeping bag and a drawing and we said we'd tell someone and we didn't. We went and had chips instead."

"We were going to. Tomorrow. We were going to—"

"Leo." Moose's voice was quiet, and in its quietness was something Leo had never heard before—not anger, not disappointment, but a weariness that was older than sixteen, that came from a place deeper than the investigation or the mystery or the game they'd been playing. "We saw that drawing and we had chips and we didn't do anything. And he's been sleeping there."

Callum was watching them. His expression was unreadable—caught between the awkwardness of being the subject of someone else's argument and the raw, exposed feeling of having just told two near-strangers the worst things about his life.

"Mate," Moose said, turning back to Callum. "How long? How long have you been going to the pump house?"

"A few weeks. When mum's on nights. Lily's asleep by eight, so I go after that. I'm back by midnight."

"And Lily? Your sister? She's alone?"

"She's asleep. She's fine. She doesn't wake up."

"She's twelve."

"She sleeps through anything."

Moose closed his eyes. When he opened them, they were bright with something that Leo recognized—fear, maybe, or guilt, or the particular emotion that comes when you realize that the thing you've been treating as entertainment is actually someone's life, and you've been watching it instead of helping.

"Leo," Moose said. "We need to tell someone. Now. Not tomorrow. Now."

"I know."

"Do you? Because two days ago you said 'tomorrow' and then we ate chips and played Xbox and went to bed and did nothing, and he was in the pump house while we were doing nothing."

The words landed. They landed in the space between them and stayed there, heavy and unresolved, and Leo felt them hit—not like a punch, but like something slower, something that seeped, a bruise that wouldn't show for hours but was already forming beneath the skin.

"Moose—"

"I'm not having a go. I'm just saying what happened. We saw something real and we treated it like part of the game, and it's not a game, and it hasn't been a game since we saw the drawing."

Callum stood up. His sandwich fell off his lap and landed on the bench, forgotten. He looked between them with the expression of someone who has accidentally started a fire and is watching it spread.

"I should go," he said.

"No," Moose said. "You should sit down. We're going to the office. All three of us. We're going to tell Mr. Rudge, and he's going to call your mum, and then someone's going to help. That's what's happening."

"But—"

"Callum. Sit down."

Callum sat down. He looked very small on the bench, very young, very much like a fourteen-year-old boy who had been carrying something too heavy for too long and had finally put it down and discovered that putting it down was almost as hard as holding it.

Leo stood there. He stood there with the hot thing in his chest and the bruise that was forming and the words Moose had said sitting in the air between them like smoke, and he thought about chips and Xbox and two days of doing nothing, and he thought about Callum in the pump house with a sleeping bag and a tin of beans and a child's drawing of a home, and he thought about his own bedroom with its toast smell and its bookshelf and its duvet that Karen washed every week, and the distance between those two things—the distance between Leo's bedroom and Callum's pump house—was measured in choices, in what you do when you see something real, and Leo had made the wrong choice, and Moose had called him on it, and the calling hurt more than anything had hurt in a long time because it was true.

"Okay," Leo said. His voice was strange—thin, scraped, not his voice at all. "Okay. Let's go."

They walked to the office. Three boys on a bench, now walking through the school corridor in the sickly yellow light, past the classrooms and the lockers and the sign that read WEFTON HIGH in letters that looked like a ransom note, and none of them spoke, because the silence was doing the work that words couldn't—holding the guilt and the shame and the dawning, terrible understanding that the world is bigger than your story about it, and that being a good person isn't about having the right intentions, it's about what you do when the intentions meet the reality, and sometimes you fail, and the failure is part of the story too, and the story doesn't care about your feelings, it just keeps going, and you have to keep going with it, carrying the things you've done and the things you haven't done and the weight of both.

At the office door, Moose stopped. He looked at Leo. His face was calm—settled, resolved, the anxiety banked for once, replaced by something steadier.

"I'm not angry," he said.

"Okay."

"I'm just tired."

"I know."

"Of the game."

"I know."

Moose nodded. Then he pushed open the office door, and the fluorescent light inside was the same sickly yellow as everywhere else, but it felt different—cleaner, maybe, or just more honest—and the receptionist looked up from her computer and said "Can I help you?" and Moose said "We need to speak to Mr. Rudge" and his voice didn't waver, not once, because Moose was the better friend, and they both knew it, and neither of them said it, because some things don't need saying, they just need doing.

And Leo stood behind him, carrying the bruise, and followed.
